findings.quote: some need fasting, timing to the menstrual cycle, or stopping biotin and steroids
findings.explanation: Lists 'stopping ... steroids' as test preparation. People on regular prednisolone, hydrocortisone or dexamethasone (and some on long-term high-dose inhaled or injected steroids) must not stop them unless the prescribing doctor says so: sudden withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis, the very condition these tests look for. Any steroid hold before a 9 am cortisol or Synacthen test is set and supervised by the endocrine team. The next sentence also overstates that steroid medicines of any kind 'invalidate the result' (prednisolone can cross-react in some cortisol assays and dexamethasone does not; creams and low-dose inhalers rarely matter).
findings.suggestedFix: Delete 'and steroids' from the things to stop. Say that the person should tell the team about every steroid medicine (tablets, inhalers, creams, injections) because some affect the result, and should never stop or change a steroid unless the prescribing doctor tells them to. Soften 'invalidate the result' to 'can affect how the result is read'.

findings.quote: Kidney damage: start or intensify an ACE inhibitor/ARB, control blood pressure and glucose
findings.explanation: Written as an instruction, and as if any persistent ACR of 3 mg/mmol or more calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB. In NICE NG203 these are offered to adults with CKD at ACR 3 or more only when they have diabetes; with hypertension the trigger is ACR 30 or more, and otherwise ACR 70 or more. They are also unsuitable in pregnancy and need creatinine and potassium monitoring. The 3 and 30 cut-offs elsewhere on the page also have no threshold record (UK units, mg/mmol).
findings.suggestedFix: Describe instead of instructing, e.g. 'A persistently raised ACR marks kidney damage; the treating team uses the ACR, blood pressure and diabetes status to decide on kidney-protecting medicines such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs or SGLT2 inhibitors.' If cut-offs are kept, add UK threshold records citing NICE NG203.

findings.quote: Target 48-58 in treated diabetes
findings.explanation: The page's own threshold records give treatment targets of 48 mmol/mol (lifestyle or one drug that does not cause hypoglycaemia) and 53 mmol/mol (a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia), from NICE NG28. 58 mmol/mol (7.5%) is, as I recall, the NICE level at which to intensify treatment, not a target ceiling, so '48-58' disagrees with the records and loosens the target by 5 mmol/mol. For adult type 1 diabetes NICE NG17 aims for 48 or lower, so one range for 'treated diabetes' is also too broad.
findings.suggestedFix: Use the record values: 'Individualised; commonly 48 or 53 mmol/mol in adults with type 2 diabetes (see thresholds), tighter for the young and newly diagnosed, looser for frail or older people'. Do not state a range that is not in the records.

findings.quote: Below 0.7 defines airflow obstruction (asthma, COPD)
findings.explanation: Contradicts the `what` field, which says a result is abnormal when it falls below the lower limit of normal 'rather than below a single fixed number'. The fixed 0.7 ratio (UK NICE NG115 and GOLD, measured after a bronchodilator) and the lower limit of normal (ATS/ERS; avoids over-diagnosing obstruction in older adults) are different rules, and the page states both without saying which applies. 'Post-bronchodilator' is missing, there is no threshold record, none of the three cited references is NICE NG115 or NG245, and 'defines airflow obstruction (asthma, COPD)' is loose because asthma obstruction varies and a normal ratio does not exclude it.
findings.suggestedFix: State one rule with its jurisdiction, e.g. 'In UK COPD guidance a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7, with typical symptoms, confirms airflow obstruction; many laboratories also report a lower limit of normal'. Make the `what` sentence agree, and add a threshold record citing NICE NG115.

findings.quote: Subclinical hypothyroidism; treat if symptomatic, pregnant or TSH very high
findings.explanation: Gives a treatment rule as an instruction and omits that a single raised TSH with normal T4 is normally repeated (it can be transiently high, for example after illness) before any label or treatment. NICE NG145 does not say 'treat if symptomatic': as I recall it suggests considering levothyroxine when TSH is 10 mIU/L or more on two occasions about three months apart, a time-limited trial in adults under 65 with symptoms and a lower TSH, and caution in older adults; pregnancy follows specialist protocols. 'Very high' is unquantified.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Subclinical hypothyroidism: usually confirmed by repeating the test after about three months; whether to treat depends on the TSH level, age, symptoms, antibodies and pregnancy (NICE NG145)'. Avoid 'treat if'.

findings.quote: Heart failure and valve disease effectively excluded
findings.explanation: False reassurance. A normal resting echo makes heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and significant valve disease unlikely, but it does not exclude heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (diastolic dysfunction or filling pressures that rise only on exertion), exercise-related or intermittent problems, or a cause of breathlessness outside the heart. The same page lists diastolic function as a component and says echo cannot explain breathlessness when the heart is normal; diagnosis combines symptoms, natriuretic peptides and imaging.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Normal study: makes reduced pumping function and significant valve disease unlikely at rest; if symptoms persist, further tests such as stress imaging or natriuretic peptides may be considered.'

findings.quote: normal below 5.6 mmol/L
findings.explanation: 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) is the American Diabetes Association cut-off for impaired fasting glucose, shown here without jurisdiction and with no threshold record. WHO uses 6.1-6.9 mmol/L; NICE PH38 (as I recall) uses 5.5-6.9 mmol/L for 'high risk', with HbA1c the usual UK route. None of the cited references (MedlinePlus, WHO fact sheet, NHS type 2 page) gives 5.6. The same cut-off is repeated in interpretation[0] ('Fasting 5.6-6.9 mmol/L'), and the 7.0, 11.1 and 4.0 figures also lack records.
findings.suggestedFix: Add threshold records with jurisdiction and source (UK: NICE PH38 fasting 5.5-6.9 for high risk; WHO 6.1-6.9), or drop the 'normal below' value and the prediabetes row and point to the HbA1c page for UK prediabetes (42-47).

findings.quote: Hypoglycaemia: usually insulin or sulfonylurea excess; treat with fast sugar
findings.explanation: An instruction on a test-interpretation page, with no limits. 4.0 mmol/L is the UK alert level for people with diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas (below 3.0 is clinically significant); outside diabetes, hypoglycaemia is diagnosed at a lower level with symptoms. Fast sugar by mouth is only for someone who is alert and can swallow safely; a person who is drowsy, confused, fitting or unconscious needs emergency help (999, glucagon), and the line has no urgent-care signposting. No threshold record.
findings.suggestedFix: Describe rather than instruct: 'Hypoglycaemia in people on insulin or sulfonylureas (UK alert level 4.0 mmol/L); mild episodes are treated with fast-acting carbohydrate as in the person's care plan; confusion, drowsiness or a seizure is an emergency (call 999)'. Link to the first-aid page and add a record for 4.0 with source and jurisdiction.

findings.quote: Hypoxaemia; oxygen and urgent assessment
findings.explanation: The finding is 'SpO2 below 92% on air'. A blanket 'oxygen' below 92% conflicts with the same page's statement that 88-92% is the target in people who retain carbon dioxide: for them 90% is on target and uncontrolled oxygen can cause harm. 'Below 92%' also fits neither common UK reference point (BTS target 94-98% for most acutely ill adults; the NHS home-oximeter advice, as I recall, treats 92% or below as the emergency level). None of the three references is the BTS guideline and there is no threshold record.
findings.suggestedFix: 'A reading below the person's target range (usually under about 94% in adults; 88-92% for those at risk of carbon dioxide retention) needs urgent assessment; oxygen is given by clinicians to a target range.' Add threshold records with UK jurisdiction and source.

findings.quote: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia; urgent specialist referral in UK guidance
findings.explanation: The record (value: triglycerides above 10 mmol/L) merges two levels. 10 mmol/L is the commonly quoted level at which pancreatitis risk rises; NICE's trigger for urgent specialist referral is, as I recall, above 20 mmol/L (when not explained by alcohol excess or poor glycaemic control), with 10-20 mmol/L prompting a repeat, a search for secondary causes and specialist advice. I could not check the NG238 text, so confidence is medium.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into two records (above 10: raised pancreatitis risk, repeat and seek advice; above 20: urgent referral) after checking the exact NG238 wording and section, or soften the context to 'seek specialist advice'.

findings.quote: FEV1 improving by 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator suggests asthma rather than COPD
findings.explanation: 12% and 200 mL is the ATS/ERS definition of a significant bronchodilator response, but it does not separate asthma from COPD: a sizeable minority of people with COPD meet it, and people with asthma often fail to at a single visit (the page itself says normal spirometry does not exclude asthma). interpretation[1] ('Obstruction that reverses with salbutamol' -> 'Asthma') repeats the over-definite link. The diagnosis rests on history, the post-bronchodilator ratio and repeated or variable measures (peak flow, FeNO).
findings.suggestedFix: 'FEV1 rising by at least 12% and 200 mL supports asthma but is also seen in COPD; it is read with the history and other tests.' Change interpretation[1] to 'supports asthma'.

findings.quote: Standard culture does not grow anaerobes, fungi and some fastidious bacteria
findings.explanation: Contradicts measures[1] ('Yeasts are also reported') and the interpretation row 'Yeast grown'. Routine urine culture on CLED or chromogenic agar does grow yeasts such as Candida. What it routinely misses are anaerobes, mycobacteria and fastidious organisms (for example Ureaplasma, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia).
findings.suggestedFix: 'Standard culture does not detect anaerobes, mycobacteria or some fastidious organisms, and yeasts may grow but are not always optimally detected.'

findings.quote: Treatment and lifestyle changes are working
findings.explanation: The finding is 'Falling value'. This reads a falling HbA1c as proof that treatment is working. The page's own components and factors say HbA1c can fall falsely with haemolysis, blood loss, transfusion and pregnancy, and a fall can also accompany over-treatment with hypoglycaemia. It is one piece of evidence, read with glucose readings.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Falling value: often reflects improving glucose control, unless a red-cell cause such as blood loss or transfusion is responsible; read with glucose readings and any hypoglycaemia.'

findings.quote: Viable muscle with restricted supply, likely to benefit from revascularisation
findings.explanation: The finding is 'Reversible perfusion defect'. This overstates the benefit of revascularisation. In stable coronary disease, trials such as COURAGE and ISCHEMIA found that adding stents or bypass surgery to optimal medical treatment relieves angina but does not generally reduce death or heart attack, even with moderate or severe ischaemia on stress imaging; a prognostic benefit is limited to specific groups (for example left main disease or reduced pumping function). A reversible defect shows inducible ischaemia in viable muscle and the decision is individual.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Reversible ischaemia in viable muscle; informs anti-anginal treatment and whether angiography or revascularisation is considered.'

findings.quote: Exercise ECG alone misses a fifth of disease
findings.explanation: A pooled sensitivity of roughly 60-70% for significant coronary disease is usually quoted for exercise ECG (a third or more missed), and the next sentence calls sensitivity and specificity 'only moderate', so 'a fifth' is optimistic; none of the three cited sources (BHF, MedlinePlus, a trust leaflet) is likely to give it. UK-first point: NICE CG95 (2016 update), as I recall, no longer recommends exercise ECG to diagnose or exclude stable angina in people without known coronary disease and puts CT coronary angiography first, yet `what` and whyOrdered[0] ('intermediate probability', a US-style risk-band framework) present it as a standard first investigation.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the fraction with 'misses a substantial minority', and add a UK note that exercise ECG is no longer the first-line test for suspected angina in NICE guidance (main uses: exertional rhythm problems, prognosis, rehabilitation). Revisit whyOrdered[0].

findings.quote: two out of three samples must be positive to confirm
findings.explanation: The 'two of three samples' rule is US practice (ADA/KDIGO). UK guidance (NICE NG203, as I recall) confirms a raised ACR of 3-70 mg/mmol with one repeat early-morning sample and says a repeat is not needed if the first ACR is 70 or more. The preparation field's claim that a raised result 'is never acted on from one sample' is too absolute for the same reason. The page cites no NICE source.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with the UK rule or drop the number: 'a raised ACR is confirmed on a repeat early-morning sample, and CKD is diagnosed only when it persists for three months'. Qualify 'never' in preparation.

findings.quote: a hormone made by the placenta from about a week after implantation
findings.explanation: hCG is made by the trophoblast (the future placenta) from implantation itself and is detectable in blood within a few days, roughly 8-11 days after ovulation. 'A week after implantation' would be around the missed period and contradicts the same paragraph ('appears in blood and urine within days of the embryo implanting').
findings.suggestedFix: 'a hormone made by the cells that become the placenta, starting when the embryo implants about a week after conception'.

findings.quote: a blood test gives a number that should double every two days in a healthy early pregnancy
findings.explanation: Early-pregnancy hCG typically doubles about every 48-72 hours, more slowly once levels are above roughly 1,500 and especially above several thousand; early-pregnancy guidance judges the trend by a minimum percentage rise over 48 hours (commonly quoted around 50-65%), not a strict doubling. 'Every two days' invites readers to treat a normal, slower rise as failure, and the row 'Serum hCG rising slowly -> Failing or ectopic pregnancy' is too definite because a single slow rise is not diagnostic and viable pregnancies can rise slowly.
findings.suggestedFix: 'usually roughly doubles every two to three days in early pregnancy; doctors judge the trend over repeat tests together with ultrasound'. Soften the interpretation row to 'may suggest'.

findings.quote: or from steroid-like hormone production elsewhere
findings.explanation: The non-pituitary, non-adrenal cause of Cushing syndrome is ectopic secretion of ACTH (rarely CRH) by a tumour such as a small-cell lung cancer or carcinoid. ACTH is a peptide hormone, not 'steroid-like'.
findings.suggestedFix: 'or from a tumour elsewhere making ACTH (ectopic ACTH)'.

findings.quote: Glomerulonephritis; urgent specialist referral
findings.explanation: The finding is 'Protein with blood'. This overreaches: protein plus blood on a urine test has many ordinary causes (urine infection, fever, exercise, menstruation, stones) and the page's own limitations say temporary causes must be excluded by repeat testing. NICE NG203 refers a persistent combination (for example ACR above 30 mg/mmol with haematuria) for specialist assessment; it does not make every pair urgent. Inconsistent with urinalysis, whose equivalent row says 'Glomerular disease: needs kidney function tests and specialist review'.
findings.suggestedFix: 'Persistent protein with blood can point to glomerular disease and prompts kidney function tests and specialist assessment (urgency depends on eGFR, ACR and symptoms)'; align the urinalysis row.

notes:
No web access used. More than 20 candidates were found; the 20 above are the ones I would bet on, ordered by severity then confidence. Findings marked medium confidence rest on UK guidance wording I recall but could not check offline (NICE NG145, NG203, NG238, CG95, PH38, BTS oxygen guideline).

ONLY hba1c and lipid-profile carry thresholds records in this slice (verified in content/tests.json). Every other numeric cut-off in prose has no record, so under the brief each is a finding of its own; I raised the ones that were wrong or risky and list the rest here with their likely jurisdiction: blood-glucose 7.0 / 11.1 / 75 g OGTT (WHO/NICE, fine as stated); kidney-function-tests eGFR 90/60/15 (agree with the creatinine-egfr records for 60 and 15; 'over 90 normal' only holds without other markers of kidney damage); urine-protein ACR 3/30 and PCR 300 mg/mmol (UK, NICE NG203/KDIGO, fine as stated); urine-culture 100,000 CFU/mL (UK laboratories commonly treat 10^4 as significant in symptomatic patients); hormone-tests urate 360 / 300 micromol/L (UK BSR/NICE CKS, plausible, but no gout reference is cited); echocardiogram LVEF 55% / 40% (BSE/ESC/NICE, fine); pregnancy-test 20-25 IU/L (fine); pulse-oximetry 95-100% and PaO2 8 kPa (fine); holter-monitor 3 second pause (fine); lipid-profile 'Ideally below 5' and HDL 1.0/1.2 (UK general advice, no records). Suggest adding records with jurisdiction for the ones that drive decisions.

ALSO NOTICED, NOT LISTED BECAUSE OF THE 20 CAP (all low):
- tests/ecg interpretation[0] 'STEMI: an artery is blocked, needs emergency angioplasty' (ST elevation needs voltage criteria and exclusion of pericarditis, early repolarisation and bundle-branch block; NICE NG185, which the page cites, allows fibrinolysis when PCI cannot be delivered in time); interpretation[2] 'Tall peaked T waves: High potassium, needs immediate treatment' presumes the cause (the blood result decides); limitations and cannotTell 'a third of heart attacks have a normal first ECG' is not supported by the two cited references.
- tests/echocardiogram measures[2] 'A segment that does not move marks scar from a previous heart attack' and interpretation[2] (acute ischaemia, stunning, bundle-branch block or pacing also cause it); interpretation[0] 'Ejection fraction 30% ... start heart-failure treatment' is an instruction.
- tests/urinalysis interpretation[1] 'Blood and protein together: Glomerular disease' (same overreach as the last finding).
- tests/liver-function-tests measures[4] 'slow clotting means poor synthetic function' (vitamin K deficiency, warfarin and DOACs also prolong the INR; the page's own component row says so); components AST 'alcohol-related if AST exceeds ALT' (the usual teaching is a ratio above about 2; AST above ALT also occurs in cirrhosis of any cause).
- tests/thyroid-function-tests preparation 'biotin supplements ... should be paused for two days' (about 48 h suits low doses; high-dose biotin needs a longer washout per laboratory advice) and how 'take levothyroxine after the sample' are instructions; better as 'laboratories often advise'.
- tests/spirometry preparation 'Avoid inhalers ... before the test as instructed' is hedged but should say to follow the lung-function department's instructions and not stop regular treatment otherwise.
- tests/electrolytes urlAliases 'bone-profile' is a different UK panel (calcium, phosphate, ALP, albumin); 'basic or comprehensive metabolic panel' with chloride and anion gap treated as routine is US-style (UK U&E is usually sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, with or without bicarbonate).
- tests/kidney-function-tests medicinesNote 'trimethoprim raises creatinine without harming the kidney' (it also raises potassium; a rise should not be assumed benign); preparation 'None; avoid ... a large meat meal' contradicts itself.
- tests/hba1c interpretation[0] 'Diabetes (if no condition affecting red cells)' omits the repeat-to-confirm step in thresholds[0]; components[0].measures 'Percentage of haemoglobin ... reported in mmol/mol' is a unit slip (mmol/mol is not a percentage).
- tests/urine-culture interpretation[0] 'Pure growth of E. coli ... Confirmed infection' ignores symptoms and sits against the 'Growth without symptoms' row.
- tests/hormone-tests measures[0] 'highest at 9 am' (cortisol peaks on waking; 9 am is the sampling convention); reference 'NHS: Addison's disease diagnosis' links to the condition overview rather than a diagnosis page (low confidence).
- tests/lipid-profile: HDL 'Higher is protective' is contested (raising HDL-C has not cut events). I could not verify from memory that NG238 states the secondary-prevention goal of LDL 2.0 / non-HDL 2.6 or the section pointers '1.9 Statin therapy: targets' / 'follow-up'; worth a check against the guideline.

SITE-WIDE LABELS: 'Anterior cusp of aortic valve' (echocardiogram structures; also in anatomy, first-aid and terms files) - aortic valve cusps are right, left and posterior (non-coronary); 'anterior' belongs to the pulmonary valve, though this may be an atlas naming convention (low confidence). thyroid-function-tests lists 'Thyroid cartilage' (a laryngeal cartilage) as a structure and no thyroid gland, and liver-function-tests links lung-cancer; both look like tagging quirks.
